doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Leaving Springfield and New York; his mother's support
summary: Music let him leave Springfield and New York; his mother was his fan, including a Birdland night introducing her to Buddy Rich.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well really it was music — music really allowed me to get out of Springfield and get out of New York. I mean I was a kid — sometimes I thought I would never get out of New York. Even though I loved it and everything, it’s so huge and so intimidating at times, it’s like, especially when I was living in Harlem. When you live in Harlem, though you love it and everything, you know people yourself who have never gotten out of there. So it’s sort of like kind of am I in this situation? I mean I wasn’t a rich college kid living in New York, I was just trying to struggle with making a living and learning how to play, and you sort of can get like whoa man, this is a little bit too big.
Did your parents think you were pursuing a dead end?

Naa. No, quite the opposite. Because the thing is I never — I always made a buck you know. And I was never the type of kid that was like — you know if I wasn’t making music playing, making money playing music, I’d go out and get a job. And so my mom was like a real, like a Eddie Marshall fan.

I mean this woman was just too much. I mean I would come home, even early there, I’d come home and practice. And I was really gone. Once I got into it I mean I was a maniac, I’d practice all the time. And she was just totally into it. And I’ll never forget one night we were at Birdland. I forget who I was with, oh probably with Toshiko. And we were opening for Buddy Rich’s band. And so we were up there and I played and everything and I says, “Mom, we’re going to sit and listen to Buddy Rich.” So we were watching and listening to Buddy Rich and he’s killing it. I mean, you know Buddy Rich. And I knew him. So I said, “I want to introduce you to him.” And he was always nice to me. And I said, “I’d like you to meet my mom.” And the first thing she says, “Well did you hear Eddie play?” And he’s like taking it all down and everything. And she said, “Wasn’t it a wonderful solo?” And I’m saying, “Mom, please, you know, chill.” And I was a little embarrassed. I couldn’t believe it. But she was like that. And I have a brother, twenty years younger than me, Ricky, and he’s a drummer also. And he started playing and she was the same way with Ricky. And no, I mean I loved it a lot and I wasn’t going to do anything else anyhow.
Right. Well it’s nice to have that on your side, isn’t it.
